summary: Defines a standard set of field names, called the Electronic Commerce Modeling Language version 1.1, for the information that online merchants ask customers to type in. With common fields, wallet software can fill in forms automatically, and manual entry is less confusing too.

plainLanguage.summary: ECML 1.1 gives online forms shared names for information such as a shipping address or card number. A wallet can use those names to fill in fields across different merchants. The RFC also defines fields that let a merchant send transaction details back to the wallet.

questions: standard fields for online checkout forms
ecml field names for online checkout
subtitle: Shared field names let electronic wallets fill online checkout forms across merchants.

tldr.problem: Online merchants used different field names and layouts for customer information, making checkout tedious and wallet software difficult to use across sites.
tldr.mechanism: ECML 1.1 defines common field names for shipping, billing, payment, account, and transaction data. The names can be used in HTML forms or an XML encoding, and the RFC adds fields for messages from merchants to wallets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3106 obsoletes ECML 1.0 in RFC 2706 and has been updated by RFC 4112. ECML defines fields, not payment technology, and does not replace TLS, SET, XML, or IOTP.

today: RFC 3106 is Informational. It obsoletes RFC 2706 and has been updated by RFC 4112. Its IESG note said ECML version 2.0 was under development when this RFC was published.

sections.title: Why Common Checkout Fields Help
sections.content:
Merchants often asked customers to enter substantial information in online forms, but their field names differed. The RFC reports that around two thirds of merchant forms were abandoned during fill-in.

An electronic wallet stores billing, shipping, payment, and preference information and can use it to complete forms. ECML gives merchants a shared set of field names so wallets from different vendors can recognize the same kinds of information.
sections.plainLanguage: ECML gives forms consistent names for customer information. Wallet software can recognize those names and fill in the matching details.

sections.title: Customer and Payment Fields
sections.content:
Customer-to-merchant fields cover shipping, billing, and receipt addresses, along with payment-card and account information. Field names use underscores to show their hierarchy, such as Ecom_ShipTo_Postal_Name_First.

The Min column specifies the minimum space a form should allow, not the minimum length of a valid value. Merchants may need to accept longer or shorter entries. For example, the card-number field has a minimum entry size of 19 characters, and the postal-code field has a minimum of 14.
sections.plainLanguage: The field list groups related details, such as parts of a shipping address. Its size guidance tells form designers how much room to allow, not which values are valid.

sections.title: HTML Forms and XML Encoding
sections.content:
ECML defines field names rather than one required transmission format. In HTML, form input names match the ECML list; the RFC requires support for text, hidden, and password input fields, as well as select fields.

The document also provides an XML document type definition for grouping the same data into elements such as ShipTo, BillTo, and Payment. The XML rules require support for UTF-8 and UTF-16 and allow an xml:lang attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A merchant can use ECML names in an HTML form or represent the information in XML. The names stay consistent even when the format changes.

sections.title: Using ECML Across a Transaction
sections.content:
Merchants choose which fields to request and when to request them. ECML 1.1 does not mark fields as mandatory, so customer software treats every field as optional even though the merchant may ask again if required information is missing.

Every web page containing ECML fields must include Ecom_SchemaVersion, whose value for this version is http://www.ecml.org/version/1.1. A final-page Ecom_TransactionComplete field tells multi-page filling software when to stop.

Merchant-to-customer fields can carry details such as a transaction identifier, amount, currency, date, and signature. The RFC does not specify the format of receipt signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema-version field tells a wallet which ECML field set the page uses. A completion field can tell it to stop filling when the transaction ends.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Many ECML fields contain sensitive data. The RFC says such data should be protected when sent over the public Internet or another observable channel, and names TLS/SSL or IPsec as examples of channel protection.

Wallet users need control over when information is released. A wallet on a shared terminal should be configurable to disable stored contact information, and stored information should be protectable by a password. Multi-page automatic filling should stop when it encounters the transaction-complete field until filling is authorized again.
sections.plainLanguage: ECML forms can carry private details, so users need control over where wallets store them and when they release them. The RFC recommends protecting data while it travels across observable networks.
